national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) – Portal: Business Registration Online (BRO), My Business Account (MyBA), and Represent a Client; Alberta provincial registry does not administer tax IDs for GST/HST or corporate income tax.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign entity establishing an Alberta Limited Partnership must first obtain a Business Number (BN) from the CRA as the master identifier, then register for a GST/HST program account. The Alberta LP file is administered by the Alberta Corporate Registry, which issues a Certificate of Limited Partnership; that certificate and a completed Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number) are required. A non-resident LP may be required to provide identification details of all partners and may have a deemed non-resident partner account for Part X.III tax and withholding under Form NR6/NR4 procedures. Registration is mandatory if the LP is carrying on commercial activity in Canada and not a small supplier, or if making taxable supplies connected with Canada that exceed the small supplier threshold.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada has no US-style check-the-box election. An Alberta Limited Partnership is fiscally transparent for income tax; each partner includes its share of income/loss on a calendar-year basis from T5013 schedules. For GST/HST, a partnership is treated as a separate person by reason of Excise Tax Act (ETA) section 240, and is jointly and severally liable with its partners. Optional elections include: (1) application to register as a GST/HST registrant under ETA section 240(1) if the partnership is a small supplier; (2) election to have a common GST/HST fiscal year end; (3) for non-resident partners, election under Income Tax Act section 216 to file a Canadian return on net rental income; (4) agreement to reallocate income among partners if the partnership is used as a conduit for hybrid mismatch transactions, subject to anti-avoidance recharacterization under Income Tax Act section 18.9 and the ETA's general anti-avoidance rules. No elective hybrid mismatch 'check-the-box' exists in Canadian law.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax) – Alberta applies only the federal 5% GST because it has no provincial sales tax or HST component.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in total worldwide taxable supplies (GST/HST small supplier threshold). For non-resident suppliers, once the LP's global taxable revenues exceed CAD 30,000 in the applicable four calendar quarters, GST/HST registration is mandatory if it makes taxable supplies in Canada. Supplies of recycled scrap copper for export may qualify as zero-rated, but the entity must still register if turnover exceeds the threshold.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time national fiscal clearance or tax authority digital stamping mandate exists in Canada. The CRA accepts electronic invoices provided they contain prescribed GST/HST information (vendor BN, date of supply, total consideration, GST/HST charged or payable, vendor and purchaser names). A general-information invoice is required for taxable supplies above CAD 50. The Pan-Canadian E-Invoicing Framework (PCEF) is voluntary and based on Peppol BIS; it does not impose clearance obligations. Record retention is electronic or paper for six years; CRA may demand documents, but no pre-clearance API validation is required.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating under ETA Schedule VI, Part V applies to a supply of tangible personal property (including recycled scrap copper wire) that is made in Canada to a non-resident recipient and delivered to a destination outside Canada, or exported by the supplier or a common carrier. The supplier must retain satisfactory proof of export within the statutory documentation period (normally two years from the date the return is filed). For cross-border commercial consignment, this includes an executed sales agreement, shipping records, and evidence that title and risk of loss pass outside Canada. The zero-rated supply removes GST/HST at source, and input tax credits (ITCs) may be claimed for related inputs so long as the export substantiation file is complete.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration, Bill of Lading, Inward Remittance Certificate
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA may reassess a claimed zero-rated export within the normal three-year statute-barred period (more if the taxpayer consents) if export proof is incomplete. Technical deficiencies attract a GST/HST assessment at 5%, plus late-filing penalties and compound arrears interest under ETA sections 280-281. Grossly negligent or fraudulent zero-rating claims are subject to an additional penalty of up to 25% of the tax amount (ETA section 280.1), and criminal prosecution can lead to fines up to CAD 100,000 and imprisonment up to two years (ETA section 286). Where a penalty is assessed under CRA administrative practice, a similar penalty may apply under the Income Tax Act for fraudulent refund claims; clawback may also be imposed concurrently with 50% misrepresentation penalties under ITA section 163.2.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), in coordination with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) for prudential banking regulation and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for AML/CFT supervision. Canada maintains a fully liberalized exchange control framework; the Exchange Control Act was repealed in 1951, and no foreign exchange administration decree or central bank pre-approval regime currently applies to trade settlements, capital movements, or dividend/profit remittances.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar (CAD) is a freely floating currency with full current-account and capital-account convertibility under the IMF Articles VIII status. There are no exchange control restrictions on the purchase, holding, or transfer of foreign currency by residents or non-residents. For a non-resident-owned Alberta Limited Partnership engaged in cross-border scrap copper consignment, investor capital injections, trade proceeds in USD, and distributions to foreign limited partners are freely movable. The sole structural hurdle is the Canadian withholding tax under Part XIII of the Income Tax Act (Canada): distributions/dividends and management fees to non-residents are subject to a 25% statutory withholding rate, generally reduced under applicable tax treaties (e.g., Canada-US Article X reductions for portfolio/brother-sister limited partners). Treasury planning must include treaty-form documentation on file (NR301, or beneficial-ownership self-declarations) prior to outbound remittance. Additionally, large cross-border transfers attract statutory FINTRAC reporting thresholds: SWIFT instructions over CAD 10,000 must contain full sender/beneficiary identity, and physical currency movements over CAD 10,000 must be declared to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no mandatory surrender requirement, no minimum conversion ratio, and no statutory timeline for the repatriation or conversion of export proceeds. Proceeds from the export of recycled copper scrap can remain in foreign currency (e.g., USD) in a non-resident or domestic USD account indefinitely. The only compliance duties are accounting and tax disclosure: the Alberta LP must reflect foreign exchange gains/losses in accordance with the Income Tax Act for fiscal reporting, and convertible-currency positions are not subject to Bank of Canada reporting. Export documentation requirements arising from export of physical scrap, including customs declarations through the Canadian Export Reporting System (e.g., CBSA Form B13A / CAED), must accompany each shipment, and proceeds evidenced by corresponding SWIFT MT103 messages should be archived for anti-money-laundering proof-of-trade audits.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: LOW for primary banking / MEDIUM for peripheral FX execution. Canadian-regulated Payment Service Providers (including Wise Business, Thunes, Payoneer, and Convera) can offer multi-currency settlement accounts and spot FX conversion under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA, in force as of 2024), but none provide documentary letters of credit, trade bill acceptance, or commercial borrowing against merchandise. The recycling scrap trade requires a bank-confirmed LC or documentary collection instrument for counterparty credit mitigation; therefore, a fintech/EMI can only serve as a secondary operational rail for small USD remittances below CAD 10,000 or as a supplementary payment conduit. Legal constraint: any EMI holding funds for merchant settlement must not be used as a capital-escrow of investor funds because insured deposit protection under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) is limited to Schedule I chartered banks, and LP capital contributions routed via an uninsured EMI would violate standard LP agreement escrow clauses.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote opening is permitted for a Canadian LP provided at least one authorized signatory (a principal of the General Partner) completes a live video identification (FINTRAC-compliant) and is a Canadian resident or a foreign resident with notarized identification acceptable to the bank. In practice, all major Canadian banks will require a physical branch visit or a notarized remote identity verification for foreign signatories, plus submission of: (i) the LP's Certificate of Registration issued by the Alberta Corporate Registry; (ii) the full partnership agreement with a schedule of Limited Partner capital commitments and UBOs; (iii) corporate resolution naming the authorized signatories; and (iv) an attestation confirming that the General Partner is duly registered. There is no statutory requirement for a Canadian resident director for a foreign-owned Alberta LP, but a senior compliance officer who is a Canadian resident will accelerate approval. For documentary LC onboarding, a high-touch interview (physical or video conference) with the bank's trade-services compliance team is mandatory to satisfy the enhanced-due-diligence (EDD) necessary for commodities trading.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: UBO opacity of a multi-tier Limited Partnership structure with foreign limited partners
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: (a) Current, certified copy of the Alberta Registered Partnership (LP) record; (b) the partnership agreement with schedules identifying all limited partners holding >10% economic interest and their date of birth/nationality for each UBO; (c) an organizational chart with genealogical ownership tracing from the LP through each intermediate entity to the ultimate natural person; (d) signed declarations of source-of-wealth for all capital commitments; and (e) independent legal opinion from a Canadian counsel confirming the validity of the LP under the Alberta Partnership Act and the non-reviewability of passive LP interests under the Investment Canada Act.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-risk jurisdiction exposure: scrap copper sourced from or destined for sanctioned or AML-deficient jurisdictions (e.g., high-risk flagged trade routes)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: (a) End-to-end chain-of-custody documentation including supplier commercial invoices, incoterms contracts (CIF/FOB), weight-scale tickets, and truck/rail bills of lading; (b) CBSA Customs Export Declarations (B13A) matching the LC terms; (c) independent third-party inspection certificates (e.g., SGS/Intertek) evidencing physical commodity grade; (d) confirmation that neither the exporter, consignee, nor vessel is on OSFI/DFATD sanctions lists; (e) trade route screening report from the bank's sanctions solution covering ocean vessel IMO numbers; and (f) a written sanctions-compliance policy of the LP itself.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cash-intensive and trade-based money laundering risk in recycled-metal trading (valuation opacity and weight fraud)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: (a) The LP's written AML/CFT program, including risk assessment and enhanced transaction monitoring policies; (b) audited transactional history evidencing only documentary settlements (LC/DP/DA), never cash; (c) tripartite surveyor attestation of scrap valuation referencing the London Metal Exchange (LME) published copper price at the date of negotiation; (d) warehouse receipts and insurance certificates with a declared commodity value consistent with the LC; (e) a lender/beneficiary mandate that disbursements be made strictly against presentation of compliant transport and certificate-of-origin documents; and (f) historical bank statements showing no unusual same-day in/out flows or round-trip settlements.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Consignment vs. sale ambiguity under 'physical consignment of shredded copper' potentially triggering inventory financing red flags
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: (a) Formal master consignment framework agreement distinguishing consigned inventory at destination facilities from outright sales; (b) confirmed export sales contracts with clear title-passage and risk-passage clauses; (c) periodic reconciliation reports from the consignee warehouse custodian; (d) independent custody audit certificates; (e) insurance policy schedules naming the Alberta LP as loss payee; and (f) a letter from the LP's external auditor confirming the accounting treatment of consigned inventory under IFRS 15.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Frequent high-value USD wire instructions with compressed counterparty circles in the scrap ecosystem (family office connections)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: (a) Annual compliance attestation listing all approved payment counterparties; (b) sub-limits for discretionary FX/wire releases; (c) dual authorization matrix signed by bank compliance; (d) complete payment bundles (invoice + packing list + bill of lading + customs entry) held for 5 years; and (e) quarterly review meeting minutes with the Relationship Manager demonstrating transaction-pattern transparency.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Foreign limited-partner capital contributions are routed via wire transfer (SWIFT MT103) to the LP's CAD or USD escrow account with a designated Schedule I bank. The credit-memo of the remittance must carry a clear payment purpose code consistent with Canada's Balance of Payments classification: use code '2080' (Other Investment – Intercompany/Related-Party Transfer) or the specific directory code for capital subscription of an unincorporated entity, with narrative 'Limited partnership capital contribution'. The bank will require the originating financial institution to include the LP's full legal name, the General Partner's name, and the UBO passport/LP registration reference. Canada has no CFIUS-type screening of passive LP capital injections; the Investment Canada Act (ICA) is engaged only if the non-Canadian investor acquires control of an existing Canadian business above the enterprise-value threshold (CAD 1.3B for WTO investors in 2025). Since the contribution funds a new LP that has not acquired an existing Canadian business, no ICA notification is required. Internal control: ensure that the injection is received in an interest-bearing escrow account and released only after the LP's register of limited partners is updated and the General Partner issues a capital-call receipt; the escrow should be held at the same bank to simplify anti-money-laundering tracing, and the bank will require a UBO declaration of the ultimate capital providers prior to any release to the operating account.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade settlements for scrap copper supply purchases will follow the target payment rails of Documentary LC and SWIFT TT. For Documentary LC: the Alberta LP will establish a commercial letter of credit facility with its primary Schedule I bank, issuing LCs under UCP 600 rules to foreign scrap suppliers. Disbursement is against presentation of: (i) commercial invoice; (ii) full set of clean-on-board ocean bill of lading marked 'freight collect/prepaid' as per incoterms; (iii) certificate of origin; (iv) third-party inspection certificate (for non-ferrous metal quality and weight); and (v) packing list. The bank will debit the LP's operating account upon LC negotiation or acceptance. For SWIFT TT (MT103): used for smaller value payments, advance payments after B/L verification, or distributor top-ups, with all outgoing wires linked to a purchase order and commodity invoice in the bank's trade-capture system. Payments Canada operates the Lynx high-value settlement system (for CAD large-value) and the ACSS retail clearing; US-dollar wires clear via the US Fedwire or through the correspondent network of the Canadian bank's US banking subsidiary (TD Bank US, RBC Royal Bank US, BMO Harris). Settlement timing: SWIFT TT same-day to next-day; LC negotiation typically 3–5 business days after document presentation. All cross-border disbursements must be screened against OFAC/CBSA listings, and outgoing CAD wires >$10,000 are included in standard FINTRAC reports. To mitigate inherent trade-based money laundering risk, the LP must adopt the 'recycled copper' verification protocol: match bill of lading weight against LME-grade tolerance and require the freight forwarder to confirm the shipment is 'shredded non-ferrous scrap' and not regulated hazardous waste (E-waste class 9), as export of certain scrap categories may trigger the Canadian Waste Export Control under the ECL and the Cross-Border Movement of Hazardous Waste Regulations.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: FX Spot Contracts for immediate CAD/USD conversion, commonly negotiated via bank's e-FX dealing platform, with T+2 settlement through CLS.
Vanilla Outright FX Forwards (fixed-rate forward contracts) for CAD/USD and other liquid currency pairs (EUR/USD, CNH/USD) to lock in scrap-sale proceeds and settle on a fixed future date.

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) – legally permissible for CAD against non-convertible currencies (e.g., USD/INR or USD/CNH) but hardly utilized because CAD is fully convertible; if engaged, they require an ISDA Master Agreement CSA and settlement via a netting regime under a Canadian financial institution counterparty.

Cross-Currency Swaps – permitted under standard ISDA 2002 Master Agreement for converting long-term USD-denominated trade liabilities into CAD floating-rate liabilities, aligning cash flows between USD revenue and CAD operating expenses.

FX Option Structures (zero-cost collars, range forwards) – available under a standard ISDA Master Agreement with an authorized derivatives dealer, although not listed as the primary instrument family in the bank's treasury policy; treated as cautious overlay for material transaction flows.
Currency Futures listed on the Montreal Exchange (TMX group) or through US CME Globex for CAD/USD hedging – actively permissible for Canadian corporates and LPs, with daily margin requirements.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 days after each anniversary date of the limited partnership's registration in Alberta; the return confirms the registered office, general partners, limited partners' aggregate contributions, and business address.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: A late-filing penalty is assessed after the 30-day grace period; failure to file for two consecutive anniversaries may lead to administrative dissolution or cancellation of the limited partnership registration by the Registrar under the Alberta Partnership Act.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For calendar-year partnerships, no later than March 31 of the following year; for non-calendar fiscal periods, no later than six months after the partnership's fiscal year-end.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty under Income Tax Act section 162(7) of CAD 50 per partner per month up to 12 months, minimum CAD 100; additional penalties apply for incomplete income roll-forward, foreign-resident disclosure, or inaccurate partner allocations.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No Alberta limited partnership statutory audit threshold exists under the Partnership Act (RSA 2000, c P-3). An independent audit becomes mandatory only when the limited partnership is a reporting issuer under Canadian securities laws, is subject to audit requirements under its limited partnership agreement, or is bound by lender/investor covenants requiring audited financial statements.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS is required for publicly accountable reporting issuers; privately held limited partnerships in Alberta may apply IFRS or Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE). Partnership financial records must support each partner's tax reporting in accordance with the Income Tax Act and stan- dard Canadian partnership accounting practice.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta does not require a standalone annual UBO confirmation filing for limited partnerships under the Partnership Act. The limited partnership must, however, maintain a current Register of Limited Partners and include any changes to general partners in its annual return. Under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and related CRA/AML obligations, the limited partnership and its registered agent must verify and preserve beneficial ownership information, but no separate UBO return is transmitted to Alberta Corporate Registry.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Limited Partners (names, addresses, contributions, withdrawals, and transfers)
Register of General Partners (names, addresses, changes, and authority details)
Partnership Minute Book (partner resolutions, capital-call consents, indemnity and management decisions)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: $250 - $550 USD per year for Alberta registered office and annual-return filing agent services
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: $4,500 - $15,000 USD per year for an agreed-upon audit or financial statement review; nil if no audit is required and the partnership agreement waives audit

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% (combined federal 15% + Alberta 8% general corporate rate; reference only, as LP is pass-through)
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Limited Partnership is fiscally transparent; income is allocated to partners and taxed at their respective marginal rates. No corporate income tax at the LP level. Partners may claim deductions, credits, and treaty relief as applicable.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T5013 (Statement of Partnership Income) filed via CRA's electronic filing system (EFILE/TELEFILE) or paper filing
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T5013 must be filed by the last day of the fifth month after the partnership's fiscal year-end (e.g., May 31 for a December 31 year-end).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Business income (gross revenue from scrap metal trading)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report all Canadian-source business income allocated to non-resident partners; ensure proper allocation per partnership agreement.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Business expenses (cost of goods sold, shipping, storage, administrative costs)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Deduct only expenses directly related to Canadian business operations; maintain supporting documentation for cross-border transactions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net income (loss) for the fiscal period
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate net income to each partner based on their share; non-resident partners must report this in their home jurisdiction.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Partner's share of income (loss) and tax withheld
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For non-resident partners, report the amount of Part XIII tax withheld on distributions; attach Form NR301 if treaty relief is claimed.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty of $5 per day (up to $2,500) plus additional penalties for gross negligence (up to 50% of unpaid tax). Interest accrues on unpaid amounts.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% (Part XIII withholding tax on distributions to non-resident partners)
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim reduced withholding under a tax treaty, the non-resident partner must provide a Certificate of Residency (Form NR301) to the partnership. The partnership must file Form NR302 (or NR303) with the CRA to obtain a reduced rate. A Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) from the partner's home jurisdiction is required.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory rates: 25% for royalties and interest. Treaty rates may reduce to 0% (interest) or 10% (royalties) under the Canada-US treaty, subject to conditions.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 5,000,000 (aggregate value of transactions with non-residents in a taxation year)
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not have a specific ESR regime, but the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) and substance-over-form principles apply. The CRA may challenge transactions lacking economic substance, and the partnership must demonstrate real business purpose and substance.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Willful omission of income, false deductions, or deliberate misrepresentation of cross-border transactions to reduce tax liability.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Criminal prosecution under the Income Tax Act (s. 239). Penalties up to 200% of tax evaded, fines up to CAD 200,000, and imprisonment up to 5 years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for unpaid corporate taxes under s. 227.1 if they fail to withhold or remit. Civil restitution, travel bans, and imprisonment for fraud.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating as a shell entity with no real economic activity, used to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions or avoid Canadian tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA may disregard the entity under GAAR, reassess income, and impose penalties of 25% of the tax avoided. Administrative monetary penalties may apply.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be held personally liable for taxes and penalties if they knowingly participated in the scheme. Civil restitution and potential criminal charges.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to implement AML procedures, report suspicious transactions, or maintain records for cross-border scrap metal trading, which is a high-risk sector for money laundering.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), penalties up to CAD 2 million for corporations and CAD 500,000 for individuals, plus imprisonment up to 5 years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers can be personally liable for AML violations if they knowingly or negligently fail to comply. Travel bans, asset freezes, and criminal prosecution.
